utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, sir, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry for bothering the Court so early in the morning. We have certain matters that need to be sorted out or to be clarified, administrative matters, and we would be extremely grateful if the Court could allow us 25 minutes to try and deal with those points. We need to deal with them now rather than at the break. I'm sorry to have to ask for this, I have not asked for this before, but on this occasion, without going into the details, I would ask the Court's indulgence. I tried to keep all matters short, I believe I have done that in cross-examination, I believe it will not affect the overall time table but there are difficulties that I would wish to resolve and I believe it will assist in any event the present situation in this case and the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Moore. We were on the verge of asking you to spell out in great detail the necessity, but we've decided not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will adjourn now until ten past 10.00. I'm sorry, sir, but you may have heard that there is a matter that counsel have to resolve so we need to adjourn for half an hour before continuing with your evidence. --- Break taken at 9.37 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We will continue with your examination-in-chief. You remember what I told you yesterday, to pause a few seconds before answering my questions for the reasons I already mentioned, not to repeat everything today as well. Mr. Maric, yesterday, we talked about your activities on the 18th of November, 1991 onwards. Now, do you remember your activities on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning, around 9.00 or 10.00, the commander called me, Captain Susic, that is, and he told me that a team of journalists would come to see me from SkyNews. That team had previously stayed with our unit a few times, and they were actually recording events for SkyNews. He told me that they would come, and I should take them where they wanted to go. Before they came, I issued an order to the company officer to get our equipment because it had been dislocated and it was in several places. So they were supposed to clean it, get it in order, in order to change the location. When the SkyNews TV crew came, since we knew each other from before, after a while, (redacted), that team -- or rather, crew and I went in the same direction where we had gone previously, and we took them to the water tower. From the water tower, they filmed the panorama of Vukovar. Van Lynden has suggested that I make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting, Mr. Maric. There is a reason why I'm doing that. So I'm asking you not to talk about what happened at Vodotoranj now. I'm interested in the actual time frame. How long did it take you to get there, and how much time did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came to Vodotoranj around mid-day, and we stayed at the water tower for about an hour; that is to say, until about 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After that, with that TV crew of SkyNews, did you go to other parts of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They asked to have a look at the centre of Vukovar and perhaps to the hospital, to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, can we move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, after the water tower, you went to the centre of town and then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went to the centre of town. We stopped on the way so that they could film destroyed buildings and the general situation. I did not allow them to leave the car, because I was not sure whether there were any left-over mines or anything like that. Along the way, we came across a French TV crew, who they knew, and they asked to come along with us. As we were moving towards the centre, Van Lynden asked to stop at the hospital. That was outside my zone. I called the command to ask whether I could take him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, would you please explain who Van Lynden is? You said something about them being with you before. Could you explain these contacts?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Van Lynden is a SkyNews journalist. They came -- well, I was absent. That was the first time they came to the unit, probably someone let them come there. So two or three times they did some filming with the unit. When I returned after my wounding, a few days after that, they stayed with us and spent a night there, too. It was a crew of five or six people. I think that's the way you pronounced name, Van Lynden. I am sorry if I'm mispronouncing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This time that you spent with him before the 19th, you said that they spent a night with you there. Did they see the combat positions? Were there any restrictions imposed on them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no restrictions imposed on them. It's as if they were part of our unit. That is the way they were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, let us now go back to their wish to see the Vukovar Hospital, because you say it wasn't in your zone of responsibility. You called the command, and then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Panic answered, and I told him that they wanted to go to the hospital. The hospital is on the other side of the Vuka River in the northern part of Vukovar. And he said, "No problem. Take them. We've got nothing to hide." And that's the first time I got to the hospital. So in this one vehicle, there was (redacted) who was driving, and there were through or four of them from the crew and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time it was when you came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was in the afternoon, say around 2.00, something like that; half an hour earlier, half an hour later, perhaps. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened near the hospital; but before that, let me ask you whether you saw any members of the Yugoslav People's Army by the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Around the hospital, there were soldiers of the 2nd Battalion of the military police of our brigade. I know that it is the 2nd Battalion, because I saw Captain Simic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to Simic and I told him that I had approval from our command that the TV crew could film the situation around the hospital, and then we started touring the area. We came to the main entrance. I cannot recall how this happened, but at any rate -- well, we entered the hallway and then you on the staircase, we saw Vesna Bosanac who appeared, accompanied by a nurse who was interpreting. Vesna Bosanac gave an interview there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, had you ever seen Vesna Bosanac before that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Never. She introduced herself then; and since I am a Bosanac, Bosnian, I remembered her last name. She said that there were a certain number of people there in the hospital, civilians, and she suggested that the TV crew film the situation within the hospital. Van Lynden asked me whether that was possible, and I said it was possible. He asked me whether I'd come with him. I refused, since I had full gear. I was armed; I didn't want to enter the hospital that way. He went with her and I walked out of the hospital, and then the soldiers called me to see some corpses nearby. There were also some containers near the emergency entrance, and there were some parts of human bodies there and weapons. I was in camouflage uniform and they always think we are something special, but I said let it be and the organs in charge would come and investigate properly. Van Lynden came and he was quite shaken as he walked out, and pretty soon, we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long did this visit of Mr. Van Lynden to the hospital last?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could have been an hour, a bit over an hour, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything going on around the hospital, that something was going on around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know notice special. There were these soldiers there. -- Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't notice somebody trying to endanger someone in the hospital, that there were some clashes or conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of the above.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Bulatovic. I've got this growing problem with the two of you in my sight when I look in that line, that direction. You must each be flattered when I call you by the other name, but it is a leading question, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem whatsoever, Your Honour. The fact that you confuse Mr. Borovic and me, and I fully accept that this objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Maric, could you explain the atmosphere around the hospital and what he saw there. Mr. Van Lynden was in the hospital and you talked to soldiers outside?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital had been hit by artillery, and around, there was quite a lot of rubble. In front of the hospital, there was this wall, and there were quite a few corpses lined up by that wall; that is to say, that they were not scattered about as if they had been hit there, but it's as if they had been brought there. So it was an ugly scene. I mean soldiers of the 2nd Battalion were everywhere. They were at all positions, so the hospital was fully protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, after this hour, hour and a half, as you said, you left. What about the SkyNews crew that was with you, did they leave with you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were with me in my vehicle. They didn't have a vehicle of their own. We all returned together. I cannot remember now whether they stayed spending the night there, whether they went back. But I think they went back to Negoslavci straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After returning from Vukovar, did you have contact with that TV crew later?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of contacts?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw each other several times. Just after Vukovar, we had dinner together in Belgrade that was organized by Van Lynden on the occasion of his departure from Belgrade, or rather, after that particular tour of duty of his. Should I explain who attended the dinner? It was Van Lynden; his cameraman; his Belgrade producer, Mr. Kusovac; Jaksa Scekic, who also works for them. That is on our side, so to speak. On our side, it was (redacted), Miksa, and I; Sergeant Bulatovic, that is. We were at the club of the cultural and education society, and we were talking about the times as they were then. We talked about what it was like when they did the filming; and then after that, we went to Jaksic's apartment. The date was when the Red Star football team would play the Kolokolo to see who the world soccer champion would be. That's why I remember the date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question put by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any objections then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I won't speak at length, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we know what this is about. But would you tell the Trial Chamber why you remember that day, what was the sports event?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red Star and Kolokolo played a soccer match on that day. I think that Kolokolo is a team from Brazil or Argentina, and they were playing in Japan, in Tokyo. It was a game that would decide who the world champion would be. So it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Red Star?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red Star is a Belgrade football club; and at that time, they were European champions, and, indeed, they became world champions then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. We should know, just briefly, did you talk to talk to Mr. Van Lynden that moment, that evening related to his presence in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about it the whole evening, in fact, and Van Lynden had a very positive view about our unit. And he thanked us profusely for the concern that he had expressed for his work and the hospitality that we had accorded him and for having it made possible for him to achieve world fame, because SkyNews dedicated the breaking news to that particular topic that evening for ten minutes. Later, when we went to Jaksic's flat, he wanted to show me what it was that he had sent in as his reports, and what had been broadcast by SkyNews. He said that he apologised if there was any shortenings, and I saw that the editor in chief in a way edited the material that he had sent in and it was so. He submitted realistic reports, and of course the editor edited them to his -- to suit his purposes. It was not very dramatic, but it was obvious. However, when it came to the report from the hospital, I noticed that all those were filmed in the hospital were civilians, which was to say elderly people and women. And I told him that that was not fair, because he had been with us. He saw that we had fought fiercely armed groups. And now according to that footage, it turned out that we had fought some old women. Then he sent the cameraman to get all the footage from the car. And during hour that we were watching the football match, he went through the footage to see whether the abridgements had been made by the -- him or by the editor. Later, he apologised, and he said that the editing was not done by his editor but by him. It was his mistake. Because having been shaken by the situation inside, he actually filmed what he was being invited to film inside. And that is what accounted for that. And he indeed apologised a number of times, and he asked me not to bear a grudge with him because of that for the sake of some future cooperation that we might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, when did this working day, the 19th of November, finish for you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had left after dark had already fallen, and we were not want to pursue any intensive activities after that. Nothing significant, in other words, simply happened they had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we shall now move on to the 20th of November. Do you remember where you were on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that the day before, which is the 19th of November, I had ordered the warrant officer, the company commander to prepare the equipment. We had been issued with some armaments which were not our weapons but the Vukovar unit's, and that was to be returned to the unit that had signed for it. So the company commander had prepared that; and sometime around 11.00 in the morning, I went with him to the barracks where we were supposed to return the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And that barracks is where?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That barracks is in Vukovar in the -- it was to the south from the spot where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And who accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was this warrant officer, the company commander, and two soldiers to carry it. We were in just one vehicle, because there were three, or rather, four crates, boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, can you describe your arrival at the barracks, your entering the barracks, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was around 11.00 in the morning. I went through the entry and exit checkpoint. And from that gatepost to the actual building, there some 50 metres, I believe. Approaching entering, I saw a group of people, some 50-odd men in different garb. Some were in civilian clothes, others were in uniform. It was a motley group standing right there on the approach to the barracks building itself. So I stopped there and I saw Captain Predojevic, and I asked him what was going on. After I got out of the vehicle, I saw three or four buses in semi-circular formation on this clearing, and I saw some people on the buses, sitting in the buses. Predojevic said to me that these people had come there to protest, to swear at the people, curse at the people who were sitting in the buses. As those people were really saying things and that, as far as I can remember, were in the sense of requesting that those prisoners, those people who were on the buses, they said that they were criminals, that they should be put on trial, that they had committed crimes against them, and that they should actually be the one to put them on trial and that we, on the other hand, would be liberating them or exchanging them, and that we were reds, commies. And this is the kind of language they used and this is the kind of stories they were saying. I know and knew from experience if something started like that, verbally, eventually it can grow into something much more dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please slow down, kindly.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So actually, I was trained along those lines, and I had experienced that myself in practice. So on that basis, I decided to help my colleague Predojevic in order for us to prevent any events from taking any such turns. So I was engaged in an argument. I actually started to argue with some of those who were the more vociferous. In the meantime, Captain Susic got there. So we had this argument for ten or 15 or 20 minutes at maximum, and eventually we managed to remove them from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, how large was this group of men around the buses?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not around the buses. They were outside the buses, in front of the buses. They were not quite in the immediate vicinity of the buses, perhaps some 20 metres away. There were perhaps 30 -- between 30 and 50 of them, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Maric, were any of those people armed in that group?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably. When I say probably, I don't really recall that specifically to have been the case, because probably no one threatened anyone with their weapons because I would have remembered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from what particular formations, structure those people were? Who were they? Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, they were local inhabitants. I said that some were in uniforms. Now whether they blanked to some units, that unit from the barracks, the reserve force, I don't know. But according to their reactions, I can tell you that they were all locals; namely, those who were manifesting such behaviour were certainly locals, those that were talking. I say that because they said things like: They killed my brother, they tortured my mother, and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you then draw any conclusion on the basis of such reactions as to who were the people, the people on the buses were?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I concluded that they were members of Croatian armed forces. Because I knew from the day before, I knew from before that on the 18th, a group had surrendered and that there were more groups. And as I was not engaged in any further combat operations, I suppose that these were people who had been taken prisoner elsewhere in other operations. Let me just mention that I know that on the 19th, the 2nd Battalion was to search, comb the sector of Mitnica, which hadn't been combed before. So I suppose that perhaps that might have been the result of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, did you have any information or knowledge related to the Vukovar Hospital apart from that, from your stay there on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had nothing to do with the hospital, nor did I learn anything in particular about it, apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As for the barracks in Vukovar, how frequently did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was my third time at that barracks. The first time I went there was when I was wounded on the 2nd of October; and they had an infirmary there, that's why I went there. Then I was there on the 17th in the evening before this attack on the 18th, and this was the third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who the commander of the barracks in Vukovar was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that moment. I found out later, but I was not interested at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that after some 15 or 20 minutes of these altercations with these people, you sent them away from the barracks compound. And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after a discussion, arguments of 15 or 20 minutes, they went away; and as the situation had calmed down, Captain Susic and I, myself, went into the building. I wanted to return the equipment that I had been issued with. Where Susic went, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, when you returned the -- the returning of the equipment that you had been issued, how much did that take?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not doing that myself. We found this warrant officer who had signed for it. So my company commander went with him to finish that particular business; and while I waited for him, I talked to some other company commanders whom I had not seen for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say approximately after suppressing this group of people, or rather, expelling this group of people, and going -- and between that and going to the command building and your stay in the command building, how much did that last?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand you. Are you talking about the entire stay, or just how long we were in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you finished returning the weapons, did you do anything else after that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After I left the barracks, those buses were not there any longer. There was nothing specific to see, so I went to my unit to see what would be happening with the equipment that we would not be returning, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask any of the commanding -- of the officers that you saw who had sent the buses, where from the buses, how come the buses, anything in that vein?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no particular discussions about that. Believe me I had other business to attend to, and I wasn't very much interested in that, if you're referring to that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, let us go back to some events that need further clarification; namely, when you returned to the unit, was there any dissatisfaction in your unit that you observed, or were informed about when you returned? Did your unit participate in combat operations at all times? If it didn't, why not? And generally what was the situation there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically, when I got there, I found that there had been some problems in the functioning of my unit. One could even say that they had refused to carry out tasks, and that that had happened towards the end of October; and that after a couple of days rest in Negoslavci, they were again fed into combat operations. I received this information from different officers at different points, starting from the Belgrade barracks when I set out on my return journey in Negoslavci up to the point of entry into the combat line itself. The first impression I had when I came and saw the way my people were looking was that they were slightly out of the ordinary. Their beards had grown, they were unshaven, they were slightly unkempt. They behaved in a -- some inappropriate ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them what the reasons for such conduct were?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, knowing the people and knowing how burdened they were, I did not directly confront them in a soldierly manner with these issues to clarify the situation. I rather went about finding out what the problems were, and basically it was their dissatisfaction with the way they had been used after I had left. They were unhappy with the sanitation conditions, the hygienic conditions, the lack of care, as they put it, on the part of the command, about their living conditions, and also that they were under friendly fire for a while; namely, that he that they had gained the impression that somebody there wanted to exhaust them to the maximum. At the same time, I have to remark that the people, who were within the area of the front line; namely, the locals and everybody else, spoke in the most laudable terms about my unit and their behaviour. And they even said that nothing would have been achieved in that area had it not been for my unit. So it was obvious to me that there had been a sort of discrepant view of the situation between my unit and the command. So I dedicated, I actually sought to revolve that problem, to pinpoint the root causes of the problem. And I concluded that the basic 10 cause of the discrepancy was the fact that (redacted) was not capable enough, mature enough to be company commander to be able -- namely, he functioned well as an individual, as a combat and individually, but he could not manage the entire command structure properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, in order not to have to move to private session any -- every now and then, and because I don't know what you will be saying, please do not refer to his name but just speak about the commander of the platoon.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I didn't know that his was a protected name. Therefore, I concluded that that was the gist of it, that there was this discrepancy consisting of the following: Whenever he reacted at the command in strong terms, he would be reacting in strong terms to what realistic assessments were or were not; and then as he went back to his unit, he would be speaking to his men and presenting them the situation in a different light.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this, if we look at the proofing notes, it says: "He will testify to the situation at the unit he found upon his return and the reasons for discontent, as well as to the situation in the unit prior to his departure to Vukovar and the so-called upheaval, in which several officers from that unit participated, as well as the reasons and events of those days." Now, we've had specific statements relating to specific individuals, conclusions as to the capability of specific -- of a specific individual, and none of that is here. This is nothing more than a conclusion that they're going to be talking about a certain incident or a certain situation. There's nothing in this proofing note that a certain person will be discussed. I will provide my opinions as to the capability of certain individuals. I will discuss who was correct, who was wrong, and the reason for that. This is outside of the proofing note. We've had no notice of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the proofing notes would serve only as guidelines for the Prosecution to know the points on which the witness will testify here. Mr. Weiner said that the proofing notes said that the witness would speak of the situation that he found as he returned there and of the reasons for dissatisfaction. And I believe that this is precisely what the witness is talking about. The reasons why the unit was dissatisfied. And I believe he is the only person who is placed to speak about this, because he was the company commander. I wasn't able to write everything that the witness would testify on. Had I been required to do so, I believe that the proofing notes would have been too long. I believe that I adhered to your instructions. If I have not, I should be given guidance to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, on that point, the proofing notes are not merely guidelines for other counsel, other Defence counsel and the Prosecution. They are, by the rules, required to identify the material facts about which the witness will speak. That's the first question that has been raised. But it turns, in my mind, to a more serious question. What is the relevance of this dissatisfaction in a particular unit to the issues concerning the three accused men, more particularly, your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the unit at hand is a unit which held a special position among the units that were engaged and under the command of Mr. Mrksic. The unit had contacts with other military formations that were present there. It had contacts with the security organ. Therefore, this witness is well placed to speak about these matters, and we have a report admitted into evidence drafted by Mr. Sljivancanin, as the security organ. And he was informing the SSNO security organ about the very fact that he had problems at the front line, precisely because the military police company for anti-terrorist activity withdrew from combat due to low morale. I was trying to establish with this witness what sort of a bearing it had, in view of the entire situation that we are discussing here in the relevant days of the 18th, 19th, and 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bulatovic, the primary reaction I have is that from the slender foothold that there was a report of your client reporting difficulties with a unit at the front line, from that slender foothold you're now seeking to eke out details of what those problems are. Your client may have made a report and somehow or other that report may have some relevance in the case. But the details of what a particular unit was doing and what its problems were, don't seem at all to touch on the issues that are material to the guilt or innocence of your client or any of the other accused. It's just getting too far away from the facts of this case. We're not trying to spell out the full history of the army at Vukovar. We're looking at a particular incident and issues, and we only want to spend time on those things that are really relevant to that. Now, have I missed something in all of that about relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is not a problem. I will move on to other questions that I believe are relevant, and we will desist from putting any further questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, who was able to issue orders to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the battalion, or rather, the acting commander of the battalion at the time issued orders to me. Of course down the -- or up the chain of command, the brigade commander can issue orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can the security organ issue you with any orders?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ does not issue any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did the organ -- did security organ, specifically Mr. Sljivancanin, ever issue an order to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw Mr. Sljivancanin only once before the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what sort of communications links you had with the command when you were receiving the orders you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit was on the strength of a company; however, through the UKT communication, we were able to communicate. I was one of the participants in the communication between the brigade and battalion commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what UKT link is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the ultra short-wave communication through various devices; and specifically in this case, we had Motorolas. This is the sort of communication that operates on short distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of communications did you have with your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also on the UKT communication, but we used a different frequency. In principle, I always carried two communication devices with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were with the unit at Ovcara on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, after the return from the barracks on the 20th, did you have any other activities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean nothing relevant. Of course we did something, but not of relevance to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have yet another topic to deal with; dissatisfaction among the troops. The witness mentioned that, but I'm not going to ask about it. I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I start, I would just like to know what my instructions are, since we had this unexpected break at the very beginning and we usually adjourn at 12.45, so are we going to have a break before that and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Domazet. It will be at about 20 to or quarter to 12.00. And after that break, we will go through. Would you prefer to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I can start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can certainly bring a break forward to about half past, if that would suit you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I am Vladimir Domazet, one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Mrksic, so I'm going to put a few questions to you on behalf of his Defence. Of course the same thing applies. Please answer once the questions are recorded in the transcript, so that we do not have any problems with the interpretation and the transcript. Mr. Maric, as you were answering Mr. Bulatovic's questions, in terms of command, you spoke about who you received your commands from; and I think that you said that in principle, your commands came from your battalion commander. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, it was Captain Susic, then Captain Susic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that that is the normal communications channel through which you get orders from the superior command, through your own commander, specifically Susic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the normal course of command, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But you mentioned that it is also possible for you to receive direct orders from the commander, the brigade commander. And you refer to a particular case like that; namely, what happened on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell me, first of all, how did you receive this order? In which way? I think that you haven't spoken about that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Via radio communications, through this device. As I explained before, I had communications through this network with the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And this order went directly from the commander, Commander Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you remember, of course, that order, or rather, what did that order contain?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to say that I'm giving an exact quotation, because I cannot remember it exactly, so I will interpret it. It said more or less: Go to Ovcara, see whether everything is all right there; and, if necessary, take measures for it to be all right, and report back to me as so what the situation is. It was along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Maric. Of course I did not expect you to give a verbatim quotation, but I wanted to hear what the core of this order was. Let me ask you something now that I should have asked you at the very outset, I think. You did not give any other statements to other organs with regard to all these events, except yesterday to Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Mr. Weiner, yes. No. I didn't give any other statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked about that, too, about time. So I would like to ask you to focus in order to remember. That order, first and foremost, the one that you referred to, when did it arrive? Was it at night-time, day-time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Night had fallen. I can remember that because until nightfall, I was at the water tower. When I was returning to my observation post, it was already dark. Now, how long did it take? Fifteen or 20 minutes from the water tower to the observation post. And how much time went by until I received the order? Not much, I think. So I assume that the order could have come between 1800 and 1900 hours, something like that, because nightfall is around 1700 hours, 1630 hours, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. I think that you spoke about that yesterday. That after all this time, it is very hard for you to give an exact time frame, and that you are safer as far as dates are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am most certain of is the actual sequence of events, of course dates fit into that. But give or take two hours, I can give a daily schedule as well, especially as things were happening at that time. I didn't think that they would be the subject of this kind of activity so much later. What we did was our regular type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you, Mr. Maric, about this, because some of witnesses here, members of your unit, spoke about a time, a particular time when they were already at Ovcara around 1800 hours. Do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it had to be later. It would be very hard precisely for us to be at Ovcara around 1800. In terms of the events, it could have been at 1900 hours, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your estimate, how much time was needed? You took vehicles, right, to travel from the centre of Vukovar to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we needed about half an hour, I think. When I say half an hour, I mean the time it takes us all to get together, to get into the vehicle, go there. I mean that's the only time I went. On the map, I see it's five, six, seven kilometres, and then given the conditions of the road, the condition of the road. But it's not that I exactly remember how much time it took.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. As you explained yesterday, you talked to a lieutenant-colonel. I assume on the basis of what you said about the content of that conversation, it didn't last very long; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends what you call long, about ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about your own impressions when entering the hangar. I'm not going to ask you specifically about that, because you explained it in detail yesterday. But on the basis of your description of these events, it seems that you didn't spend much time in the hangar either. Can you give an estimate as to how long you and your soldiers stayed there until they told you to leave the hangar together with you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Maric, after that, you said that you went out and that you came across some other soldiers who were around the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were people who had come with me who did not go inside. We have a regular procedure when we show up somewhere, where for the first time, some go to the left, some go to the right to see what's going on there; then they came back. So we all gathered together there by the vehicle, and -- well, I cannot say that they reported to me, but it was more in the form of a conversation: What's going on there, nothing in particular; what's going on there, is there anyone there, nothing special. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. It is not official reporting, but you received information from them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. In terms of what the security is around the buildings, whether there are other persons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On the basis of everything that you personally saw and heard from your soldiers, what was your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion was that the locality was quite safe; that it was not under any kind of threat; that the units that were there took measures that are appropriate in terms of the situation there; that there is no possibility for the captives or prisoners, whatever we call them, can escape; and they are not under any kind of threat. It was obvious that they were not mistreated, that they were not abused. There was nobody else there, and my conclusion was that I should not take any special, additional measures, or that I should suggest or that I should report to the command that something else was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. Could you please tell me again, if you can - because I see it is very hard for you - can you tell us in terms of time when you got out of the hangar and when you gathered together. How long were you there at that gathering until you left?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all together it could have been about an hour. It's not that I was in a hurry to leave this place. I did not want to make a decision in haste and just to leave. We stayed there; we talked for a while. And quite simply, I wanted to establish for myself that everything was all right. So our entire stay there, could have been, say, an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you are talking about your entire stay, you are talking about --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment I arrived, until I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please just wait for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm impatient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Another question. In view of the fact that you are a professional and in view of the position that you held then, do you think that Ovcara was a safe place for guarding prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If necessary, I can even explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, at the moment when the operation was over on the 18th, that was a moment that was full of adrenaline, so to speak. If I can put it that way, it was smart to get these people out of town. Because in that hangar, in this place called Ovcara, it's a clear area. There are no tall buildings. Since all Croats had not surrendered yet, we could have, perhaps, provided for the possibility of somebody trying to get those prisoners, to free them, because Croatian forces were creating incidents and were engaged in provocations. So they could have accused us of violating the Geneva Conventions and going against the grain of morality. Later on, it proved to be true during the war. They'd do something and then we would be blamed. So this was the right thing to do. Ovcara was a an isolated place, no axis from anywhere. It is a solid building without any openings. I think there was an regiment there, a strong unit at any rate. Even if they wanted to escape, they had nowhere to go. So the general assessment was this was indeed the best place for keeping prisoners of war safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. All of you together, or rather, you all went back together. All of you who set out came back together as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you have already said this, I'm not going to ask you again. You said that you informed the commander about this. When did you do it, and how did you do it? And what was it that you said to him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did that. Before I left Ovcara, I informed him that everything was all right -- well, it was a long those lines, that nothing else should be done. And he should, "All right. Go and get some rest." I remember that. I remember that sentence. So I didn't want to leave the facility before I informed him about this and so what was to be done after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inform your own commander, and did he know what task you were he be gauged in?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Susic knew. And when I returned, I told him what it was like. I did not contact him via radio; I saw him when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Now I should like to move to another topic. If you think that this is a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Thank you, Mr. Domazet. There are a number of redactions, so we resume at 12.00 and will go through to 12.45, when we will have the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we're going to continue and I hope we're going to end soon. My next question: Razvigor Virijevic, do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of my officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, recall, as you were speaking about these days, the 18th, the 19th and the 20th, do you recall where that officer slept?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have been at Pavle's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's what you said yesterday as well, when you were interviewed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not mention Razvigor. I don't remember having mentioning him yesterday, but he was at Pavle's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one more thing, is he one of the officers who were with you at Ovcara that evening?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we are going to move on to another subject. The 20th, the arrival at barracks. You mentioned that on that day, you were supposed to relieve yourself of that equipment that you had, and you went with a warrant officer and two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell me, when you came to the barracks, what happened then? Who did you report to? Was there a checkpoint there? What was the procedure in terms of entering the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is this checkpoint when entering barracks, that's where vehicles get in. There is another entrance for pedestrians. Of course, I reported there; and, of course, I first came there. I really don't understand what the point of the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So did you report there? Were you given approval to enter? There was a guard there, was there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The guard from this company of ours that was securing the barracks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood these developments properly, when you entered the compound to the barracks, you saw these buses and you saw these people who you talked about; and then you, yourself, walked up to them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you did not go to this assignment that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you practically walked up to them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I walked up to Captain Predojevic to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And when he explained things to you and as you said a few moments ago, you saw basically what the situation was. A few moments ago, you talked about your own experience in terms of the effect on masses. What did you want to do? Could you perhaps explain this a bit, this role of yours? Was it -- was it just verbal persuasion or did you issue any kind of warning?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, my experience in terms of working with masses and riots, demonstrators, goes back to the period before that in Belgrade, when we partly participated in this; and, of course, we as the members of the military police were trained by psychologist and other experts about such conduct. We did not resorted to any other resources here, except for verbal resources because nothing else was necessary, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You said -- I mean, when you say "you," you are referring to yourself and Predojevic; and then Susic came up, too. And all of you together managed to persuade these people to leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me where it was that these people went? Did they leave the barracks, the barracks compound? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They went to the KPS. The same way I got in, they went out. That was the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since these people were already within the barracks compound when you came, and you certainly don't know how they got in, but did anybody tell you, perhaps? Is there any way that you could know how it was that they entered the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I was not really asking anybody about that. I assume that the barracks was -- as it was damaged, generally speaking, I imagine that the actual fence, or whatever, was there had been damaged, too. I didn't really ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On the basis of what you have said, does it mean that as for this task that you were engaged in, together with the people who were accompanying you, that you actually set out to accomplish that task, only when these persons left the compound and were no longer around the buses?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After that, you went to the building in order to return your equipment. Did you personally do that, or was it the warrant officer and the soldiers who came with you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present up until the moment when contact was established with the warrant officer who was supposed to take the equipment; and when the hand-over started, then I left. And I let them go on with their job. It's their job, isn't it? So I thought that what I was doing was the focus of my own activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly? You left at the moment when the return of equipment started?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the area where equipment is returned. Since we came in the same vehicle, I left. The commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment was there. There were quite a few officers there who were my friends, and I hadn't seen them since the start of operations. So I wanted to see them and talk to them until this work was over, until the warrant officer finished doing what he was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. Since you were there within the barracks compound, do you remember whether you saw any officers who did not belong to your brigade? Any officers who was not in your brigade, regardless of whether you knew them personally? Did you see anybody like that? Can you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't identify anyone in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see Lukic? You, yourself, said that later on you found out that he was the commander --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Maybe I saw it him, maybe I didn't. But Lukic is a lot older than I am, and it's not that we were particularly close or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. So I assume that once the equipment was returned, that you were notified of that and that you left the barracks and went away?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And at that moment, in the yard, in front of the gate, there were no buses, there were no people, there was no one else there left; do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's right. There were no buses. There were probably some people there, but there was no unusual activity there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, as far as these buses were concerned, you said to the best of your recollection, there were three or four of them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Some witnesses here said that there were five to six buses, does that change anything? Do you allow for that possibility that there were more buses than what you said?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. It's not that I was counting them in particular, although I think that -- well, I don't know whether five or six buses can fit into that area there, but I think there were three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. A few moments ago I asked you whether you had perhaps seen some officers who did not belong to your brigade, and you said that you do not remember any such thing. Do you remember the officers who belonged to your brigade and who you saw and talked to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Predojevic and Srecko Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Of course, we are talking about the period when you were waiting for the equipment to be returned.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When that group was there, Predojevic and Srecko was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You did not see anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Susic came later, and perhaps there were some of Predojevic's NCOs, but -- well, by the buses, I saw there were some soldiers from the military police. So probably there were some NCOs there, too. I did not really contact them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just go back for a moment to when you were with Predojevic and then with Susic, and when you tried to persuade these people to withdraw and when indeed they did. My question is: Were there any other officers who were involved in that as well?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Specifically, I assume that you know Major Vukasinovic. Did you see him at that moment? Then, at all, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him very well, Major Vukasinovic. He was not there; he certainly was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the very end, let me ask you about command. You said that on the 18th, you received this order. And this way of receiving orders directly from the brigade commander, was that an exception, after all, or is it something that happened frequently? Can you remember in that period, in times of war and in times of peace?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not something that happened often to receive orders directly from the brigade commander, but it did happen. In Vukovar, it happened on the 2nd and on that day, on the 18th. There weren't any other situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the usual way of issuing orders is through the battalion commander. This was specifically Susic. My question is as follows: I'm referring to commander Mrksic. Could he transfer this kind of authority of his to some other officer, so that this other officer could issue orders to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Could you receive an order from some other officer from your brigade to whom your commander would have transferred such authority? For example, specifically Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, Chief of Staff, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. I'm just thinking about the context. When we say an order, that is a very broad concept. When somebody comes from the brigade command, who is bringing some kind of order for something. Well, of course it's possible, and that is how commands are issued. Now, when we say "order", a direct order for a specific task is always issued by a commander, one's superior officer. Now, some corrections in terms of orders, perhaps other organs from the command can already do that. The commander does not have to come in person each and every time. I can say that during my stay there, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. If I understand you correctly, you mostly received orders through the regular chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lieutenant-Colonel Panic came with some members of the command, from the staff, that he'd come to see. And of course there was something here or there, why didn't you move this a bit, why didn't you move that a bit. But this is not anything of grave significance. It doesn't really have to do with command itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that these are not special orders, but rather tasks, assignments?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a superior can always tell you that you didn't do something very well, but it's not of vital importance; whether say I put my reception desk here or whether it should be 50 metres away from here. Things like that. But that is regular thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It is well-known that you were absent for a while when the assault detachments were established. Did the orders then go through the battalion commander and commanders of assault detachments?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd, my unit was attached to the 2nd Assault Detachment under the command of Major Bajic, and it was then that I received part of my order from him. And when I came back, it was within the 5th Assault Detachment under the command of Susic, who is generally my commander. So in that instance, I received orders from the same person who was simultaneously commander of assault detachment and battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Maric. Thank you for your answers. I have concluded your cross-examination. Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm Borivoje Borovic, Defence counsel for Miroslav Radic. My first question: Do you know Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know him at the time of the Vukovar events?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind to tell us what was the axis of activities of the 2nd Assault Detachment and that of the 5th Assault Detachment at the time when you were engaged in combat?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd, when I was within the 2nd Assault Detachment, the axis stretched out from Negoslavci down Radnicka Street towards the barracks all the way down to the water tower, and that is the same as the 5th Assault Detachment which I joined upon my return.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, you came back around the 5th of November?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 5th and the 10th, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It has been established here as a fact that Milovo Brdo fell on the 10th of November. My question is: Prior to that, irrespective of the fall of Milovo Brdo, who was your neighbour on the left side?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left side, it was Captain Bojkovski from the 1st Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. On your axis of operations, was Captain Miroslav Radic present there with his company?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I came back, he wasn't; and I don't think he had been there earlier either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Were you, yourself, or your company ever along the axis of activities of the company of Miroslav Radic? Did you hear or did you see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither saw nor heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You said that you were in the hospital on the 19th of November, 1991. During that period of time when you were there, did you at any point in time see Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of November, 1991, in the barracks, did you at any point in time see Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could we briefly go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A very interesting and important question for me personally. You said that you studied the psychology of masses, that you had opportunity to do so during demonstrations when you had to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 9th of March, 1991, the opposition of Serbia held demonstrations in Belgrade aimed against the coverage, or rather, the coverage of the regime media and their write-ups?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and tell us which were then the regime media?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There has been enough so far to indicate some relevance. The question will be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But it's on the fringes of relevance, Mr. Borovic, so don't spend too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of March, 1991, I was also on the fringe. But let me tell you, I fared well after that. So what were the regime-controlled media?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio television of Serbia; and as for printed press, Politika and Borba.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about Ekspres Politika?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's part of the Politika media house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Phillip Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor. We met yesterday, and I'm going to be asking you some questions today. First, you testified that when you returned, your unit was subordinated to the 5th Assault Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Jovan Susic commanded that assault detachment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And until when was your unit part of that 5th Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of my stay in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were part of the 5th Assault Detachment until November 24th, when you returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most likely, as long as the 5th Assault Detachment existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you said as long as your stay in Vukovar, and you were in Vukovar until November 24th, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I suppose that the 5th Assault Detachment ceased to exist upon our return from Vukovar. It didn't exist in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, I'd like to show you a photograph and ask you if this is you. Madam usher, could you please place this on the ELMO. Could you look at this first and then could you place it on the ELMO. Could the witness look at it first, so he can hold it and look at it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We can look at it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you also testified today, at page 8, that you went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you turn it back on, please. Would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified today, on page 8, that you went to the hospital; and you said looking at the hospital, it was an ugly scene.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Certainly an ugly scene, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that, what you mean by an ugly scene?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building itself was damaged. In the yard, there was debris, construction debris; and in one section, there were corpses, quite a number of corpses, as I told you. So the whole site was ugly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also said that the hospital had been hit with artillery fire or artillery. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say that it was hit. I said that the building was damaged, most likely by artillery ordinates, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was your basis for believing it was most likely damaged by artillery ordinates?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see a hole in the wall. It's quite a significant damage, and it could not have been inflicted by infantry ammunition. When I say "artillery," I mean something of a larger calibre. It could have been a shoulder-fired rocket or something of that sort, Zolja or Osa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible, yes, yes. Yes, possibly mortars, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while you were at the hospital, you saw some bodies or you were shown some bodies, and you told them that the crime technicians will take care of this. They'll check it out or something to that extent; didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that no one should touch it, that competent authorities, who normally conduct on-site investigation, would come and do their regular job; following the regular procedure, prepare documentation, and everything else that is needed when one encounters corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now you were part of the 1st Military Battalion, weren't you? 1st Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the establishment terms, that 1st Company for anti-terrorist activities belongs to the 1st Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And within that battalion, there were several sections, your anti-terrorist section, but also a criminal section or a crime section; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't an anti-terrorist squad. It was anti-sabotage squad, which is something quite different, and then there was a squad for crime prevention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that crime prevention unit was responsible for criminal investigations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They conduct on-site investigations wherever needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were criminal technicians who could handle crime scene investigations in that unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to ask you something. I was not the commander of the battalion, and I don't know how it was at the time. I know that it was part of their composition. Now, as to where they were, it's really beyond the scope of my competence, and I am not competent to give you a proper answer. I know what the proper procedure is; and, that is to say, that nobody should touch anything, that competent authorities would come and do their job. Now, as to whether they were and what they did, I'm not competent to answer that question. I don't know where crime investigators were. This was not something that was under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you know within that military police battalion that you belonged to, there was a crime prevention squad that was responsible for criminal investigations including on-site investigations, as you just testified at page 50.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it existed within the composition of the unit. Now, as to whether they had remained in Belgrade, whether they were in Vukovar or in Negoslavci, I don't know how it was during that period of time, nor was I duty-bound to know that. I just told you what was the regular procedure that was to be applied when one comes across some corpses. We knew that there were people who were trained and were competent to implement the regular procedure. Now, at that point in time, I didn't know whether there, not there, whether they could come or not come, whether somebody else would order them to come or not. That was outside of my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
