utterances.text: Well, sir, two Defence witnesses have testified of hearing on November 21st that prisoners had been murdered. Were you aware of any investigation relating to those murders while the Guards Motorised Brigade was stationed in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of evidence they gave. I didn't hear that, nor did I know that that had happened. I didn't know about those investigations, nor do I think that I should have known about them. Because even had there been something, that investigation would have been carried out by somebody else. That was not within my competence. My unit was not trained to conduct investigations. Now, as to when they heard this, which were these people who testified and how they heard about this, I don't know. I had some other activities to perform and other things to think about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question was: Were you aware of any investigations, not whether you carried out any investigations. Were you aware of any investigations relating to the murders, to those murders while the Guards Motorised Brigade was stationed in Vukovar? Were you or were you not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't even know that there had been murders. Therefore, I couldn't know whether there were any investigations either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, we need now to break for the lunch adjournment. We resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Sir, you indicated that you were not aware of an investigation in Vukovar. Were you aware, in 1991 or 1992 of any investigation in relation to the murders at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't even know about the killings. Needless to say, I didn't know about the investigations either. In 1992, I had other tasks and I was not involved in this, nor did I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, you had been a member of the Guards Motorised Brigade for some 13 years; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were very proud of being a member of the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. I was proud.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And during that time, you served with all three accused in the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I apologise. I can't see the transcript on my screen. Could that be arranged, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you've known each of these three defendants for over 20 years; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not 20 years, 13 years. But, yes, I mean looking from today's point of view, then, yes, altogether 20 years, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you have to agree that this isn't a very positive or happy situation, that three leading figures in the Guards Motorised Brigade have been indicted and are here standing trial.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It is an embarrassing situation for the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for it being unpleasant, yes. But as for it being embarrassing, perhaps not for the Guards Brigade but for those who initiated it. Unpleasant, it is, yes, that is my view, but I don't think that the Guards Brigade did anything to deserve this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that there's been testimony in this court that members of the Guards Motorised Brigade participated in the beating of prisoners, as well as the murder of prisoners at Ovcara? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That some members of the Guards Brigade participated in this, that's the first I hear of it from you. That some of them participated directly as perpetrators, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that also is not what we'd call a positive moment for the Guards Motorised Brigade, is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. What can't you call a positive moment? You just said that some members took part in this. I don't know about that. But if that is indeed the case, if they did take part in this, then that certainly is not a positive thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well let's move on. We'll try to get back before we finish today. Now, sir, you don't have any records, or you didn't maintain any personal diary while you were in Vukovar, which was only a few weeks since you were injured most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't have any records.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you didn't maintain a personal diary or calendar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I have a reputation for not liking to write, even in peacetime, let alone in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, some officers will maintain a notebook which they turn in at the end of an assignment or at some point. Did you maintain a notebook while in -- an officer's notebook while in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're relying basically on your memory as to the events of 15 years ago?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you agree that since this is 15 years ago, it's difficult to provide exact times, dates, without having any writings to refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but there's no way I could have anything. Even if I had kept records, I was duty-bound to surrender it at the end, and then it would be destroyed or kept under their control. So even if I did keep any records, I would not have been able to use it as something to refresh my memory. And at any rate, it would probably not contain such details, because, normally, records contain landmarks, landmark information but no other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, if you had records -- if you had maintained records, you would have known the exact times that your unit participated in certain actions, times, places, if you had records; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you now, even had I kept records, I would have been duty-bound to surrender it in 1991. I had no right to take such records home because they are considered military secret and they would have remained in the barracks and they would have been destroyed with other documents in the regular procedure. So none of those records would have been available. Now, as for the records that I kept as a commander of a unit, normally such records are not kept for a very long time, only for some period of time and then they are destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, without any records or without any writings, for example, sir, you can't even tell us the exact date that you returned to service after you were injured. All I can state is it was sometime between the 5th and 10th of November; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But my return was of no significance. However, if needed, it can be verified. You can get medical documentation from the military medical academy as to when I was released from treatment, if this is a detail of importance for this trial. Because had it been important, I would have tried myself to get a hold of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I put it to you, sir, that without records or writings, you can be wrong as to certain dates or activities, because you don't have those records to substantiate them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because even without records, one has memory of events. All of us do. You probably didn't record when you got married, when your children were born, when you had your first girlfriend, but these are things you remember. So memories are just as relevant as record-keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, you agree that all of us are infallible. We can't be right all the time. That's why writings will help. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would that include the Chamber, this claim of infallibility? Perhaps fallible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, since you don't have records, would you agree over the last two days, you've been changing your dates and times -- I shouldn't say dates. You've been changing your times as to which things have occurred during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Even if I gave some information, I told you and I told earlier that those are approximate dates, approximate periods of times. And they can't be a huge difference. I said that there should be plus/minus two hours of margin of error and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall yesterday that you stated that you arrived at Ovcara at around 8.00 p.m., and that was at page 118. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I said that it was at 8.00. I don't remember that specifically. And now I just said that it was at 1900 hours, so the margin of error is two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. And today you said 1700 hours. And yesterday, in the interview, you said at 7.20.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't say 1700. I said that I could have left the water tower at 1700 hours, and then until I get to my place and then I got the order from the colonel to get ready. So I didn't say at 1700 hours, I said at 7.00 p.m., which is 1900 hours. Maybe it was a question of wrong interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Today you said at 1900 hours or 7.00 p.m. And yesterday, during the interview, you said that you recall that you arrived at the -- at Ovcara at 7.20 p.m. Do you agree, sir, that because you don't have records, you really don't know the exact time you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I could have said 7 hours and 20 minutes. I don't think I could have been as precise to give you the minutes. I think I could have only said that it was 7.00 or 8.00, and I told you there should be a margin of error of two hours. Even if I had kept records, I would not have been as detailed as you seem to require. Even if I worked in the space air traffic control, I would not have been as detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, would you agree that you also don't have any writings to support that you went there on November 18th; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I haven't got anything in writing that would corroborate that except for my word.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know, sir, that the war diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade Operations Group South doesn't indicate -- doesn't have any notation or listing indicating that you were ordered to go to the -- to go to Ovcara on the 18th of November. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't read the war diary of the OG South; and as far as I'm aware of how war diaries are kept, that document is meant for important events. And I don't see a reason for that event being recorded in the war diary of OG South, meaning what a unit, numbering 20 men, did where there were no victims, nor combat operations. It has nothing of importance that needs to be recorded, at least in my view. Now, other people might have a different view as to what needs to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well that is correct, sir, because ordering the elite unit, the anti-terrorist unit of the Guards Motorised Brigade to do an assessment is an important event, but that event is not listed in the Guards Motorised Brigade OG South war diary. And you know that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and there's no need for me to know that, because the war diary of the brigade was not available for me to read it. But if we are discussing the war diary, let me tell you that it is kept by operations officers. If Colonel Mrksic ordered this directly to me by radio link, the operations officer may not have known about that. They are aware of written orders, written documents; whereas, this particular instance was a very brief intervention, an event that was of no importance. It seems to be important now. But at the time, we could not anticipate that it would be so important. And I'm sure that there are numerous instances where the commander of the brigade ordered to somebody go there, get there, do this. These are things that are not normally recorded in the war diary. This is why I believe that at that time, nobody could have anticipated that that departure would have been of any significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you receive notice between 6.00 and 7.00 p.m., or shortly after 7.00 p.m., that notice would have occurred during the command staff briefing. As a result, Colonel Mrksic would have had to have left the briefing to issue that order to you. So it was a significant event if the colonel has to leave his briefing to provide or give you that order.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fail to understand. You say that there was some kind of a briefing at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There was a nightly briefing at the headquarters at Negoslavci, at the command of Negoslavci beginning at 6.00 p.m. If you received that order between 6.00 and 7.00 p.m., that means Colonel Mrksic would have had to have left the briefing to have issued that order to you directly. So it was a significant command if the commander had to leave his briefing; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That doesn't mean that he had to leave, because he gave that order to me via a radio device that he always has on him. And he could have done that before the briefing started. I don't know whether it started exactly at 1800 hours, so he could have given it to me via a Motorola. That didn't take that long. And he could have also done it in the presence of these people. There was no need for him to leave the room in order to issue this order to me, at least that's my thinking. I don't know whether that particular briefing was held at that exact time. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, if he interrupted the briefing, the command briefing, to give you that order, that's a significant event.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't say that he interrupted the briefing. I'm saying that he could have given that to me before the briefing started, and maybe there was no briefing held at that time because the operations had been concluded. I know Van Lynden told me that all the journalists came to Negoslavci in the afternoon, and that they pressured the command to let them in right away. So Colonel Mrksic probably had many other things to deal with, and I don't know if this was a formal procedure. So please do not impute to me something that I didn't say. I didn't say that the briefing was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's just speculation.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense did you mean? I did not say that the briefing was interrupted, so that an order could be issued to me; and then you are saying if he interrupted the briefing, then it must have been important. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, since you don't have records, you are also giving various times as to how long you were there. Yesterday, you said that you were there a half-hour, maybe at hour at most, at page 119. Today, you said it could have been an hour; and then you adjusted an hour, an hour and a half. Since you have no records, you don't even know how long you were at Ovcara; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how long I spent talking to you yesterday, let alone what happened then. Whether it was hour, hour and a half, I don't see what difference it makes. There is no major inconsistency. It's not like I said in one version that it was five minutes and then in the other version that it was two hours. Whether it was 60 minutes, 80 minutes, it's all close.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I put to you that since you don't have records and you are just relying on your memory, that you're omitting facts and you're making up facts to help your friends, the three accused. That's what I put to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you asking the witness to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I am putting that to him, and I am asking him to comment on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you, as Prosecutor, need to understand that to accuse somebody of inventing or lying in a case where I told you right away that I accepted it, but could not be very specific about details, I think that's improper of you. If you are trying to make allegations that my mental competency is reduced, then you need to prove this. And I would consider that an insult. I was asked to come here as an eye witness of an event to say what happened so that the truth can be established. I naturally could have learned by heart a text and stuck to it and repeat as a parrot, this was 17, 21, 32, but that is not realistic. You cannot expect someone it to remember that 15 years later. Therefore, I do not understand based on what you are claiming now that without those records, my recollections are completely worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's look at a situation yesterday, sir. At page -- you testified yesterday at page 18 -- I'm sorry, page 118. I asked who --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see it? Can I see that note. Since you said earlier that I said something was at 1700 hours and it turned out that that was incorrect, can I see the reference you are quoting now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you read English? I would be happy to show it to you. I'm reading from the transcript of yesterday's trial.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I can read English, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will read it and then show it to you. I'll have the usher show it to you. "We got out of our vehicles. I asked, "Who is commanding -- the commanding officer here. Some lieutenant-colonel was there. He was shorter than me, wore a moustache. He told me his name, but I do not remember it. I asked him what was going on there, and he briefly told me that the prisoners were there, that nothing particular was going on. We had a short discussion, and then I went into the hangar." That was your testimony yesterday at lines 8 to 13, and the lines I'm stressing is: "I asked him what was going on there, and he briefly told me that the prisoners were there and nothing was going on." May the witness please be shown that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need. This is all correct. I repeated the same thing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then at page 120, you said at lines 11 through 19: "Yes. We had another conversation for a while after I emerged from the hangar; and when my people came back to report to me, we discussed that there was nothing else around. "Q. Did that lieutenant-colonel say that there were any problems? "A. No. "Q. Did he tell you that he expected some problems? "A. Yes. He thought that something might happen in terms that it's dark. There were cornfields around, that there may be some combat action, but that was his assessment rather than a reflection of reality." Do you recall that testimony, or would you like to see that, too, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely. This is correct. I repeated the same thing today -- or rather, yesterday, not today. Without this portion about the dark, because Mr. Bulatovic asked me to be as brief as possible. Otherwise, yesterday's evidence and today's evidence are fully consistent, as far as I can see. I said that there was nothing with him. I entered into hangar and talked for five to ten minutes, talked to him and to my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that that testimony is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Those two portions that I just read is inaccurate, sir. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense would it be inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that when you asked that lieutenant-colonel if there were any problems, he told you that there were people around there who could endanger those prisoners. That's what you were told; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that he believed that there were some people there, and that's why I said that this was not a reflection of reality, but merely his opinion. That was his assessment, because my people checked and determined that there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, as a result of his statement, sir, isn't it true that you issued an order to your soldiers to shoot anyone who approaches the hangar; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my soldiers. I told him that if anyone showed up, that he could shoot at them. I didn't tell that to my soldiers. I told him that he could absolutely fire at anyone who showed up there; and I think that's what it says in the transcript, if you read it, because my soldiers were not there, there were just the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said to his soldiers in a very loud voice that they could shoot anyone who approaches the barracks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to his soldiers, but to him in front of his soldiers. So I was talking to him. His soldiers were present there, and I said,"You can shoot freely." And in fact, what I said was, "If anyone approaches this area, shoot." I said it aloud on purpose, just in case -- because at that time, I didn't know if anyone was there, but I wanted that party to hear us. And I also said that if he encountered any problems, he could call me and I would come with my people and intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to interrupt. I merely wanted to note that there may be an error, and perhaps my learned colleague erred here on page 64 -- 65 line 2. He spoke about soldiers to shoot anyone approaching the barracks. I think that my learned colleague, in fact, had in mind the hangar at Ovcara not the barracks. This may have been just a slip of the tongue, but the transcript reflects the word "barracks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. No one's infallible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you said it in a loud voice so anyone else who was out there could hear, because he had told you that there was a problem there and a threat to those prisoners; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that there was a problem, but that he believed that there was a problem, that there was a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you knew that there were locals there who were seeking revenge for the killing of their family members. You knew that; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the sense that these people were at Ovcara in the -- yes, in the sense that there were such people there in the Vukovar area; and if this is what the transcript reflects, then this is because I did not really specify. What I meant was that in this general area, one could expect this kind of danger. People, whose relatives had been killed, might do something. But this was not specifically meant to refer to Ovcara, because that was one of the reasons why the command did what they did by removing these people from the inhabited area where this danger would have been much greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor yesterday morning. We typed a transcript of 23 lines of that statement in relation to what you said. I'd like to show it to you. Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to have this translated to me, because I can see that you're now going to be referring specifically to every word. And there will be nuances that would be important, and my knowledge of English is not sufficient to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have the CD here to play for you, sir, but before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is not Lukic. Your Honour, I think that it would be fair to the witness, since the witness testified in B/C/S, then perhaps his statement could be shown to him in B/C/S, or perhaps we could hear the original tape, the original recording. Because as the witness remarked, his knowledge of English is not sufficient to be able to verify whether the translation is, in fact, accurate, so that he can really know what he's being shown here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Weiner was at the point of offering that, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, just for some background. Yesterday, you came to the office of the -- you came to this building here and gave a statement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you didn't come alone; you came with Attorney Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you sat down in a room and you gave a statement that was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sitting right next to you was Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you told the truth and you attempted to provide facts or responses to all questions that were asked.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I cooperated with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked in court yesterday whether the lieutenant-colonel told you of any problems, and you indicated "no." We would like to play the CD of your statement yesterday, and you can follow along in English or just listen. And it is 34:17 to 37:45 on the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that I have no right to address you. But because I am able to follow this in English, I think that the translation does not correspond to the original, and perhaps it would be good for this portion of the recording to be played again and for our interpreters in the booth to interpret, because the interpretation provided here on the recording from lines 13 to 18 does not correspond to the original. I'm sorry, once again, for presuming and for taking the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have no objection to that. If they would like to do it that way, that would be fine for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "I asked them what the situation was, whether there were any problems. He said something to the effect that there were some people there around this area, and he thought that they could pose a threat to them. He seemed a little bit uncertain as to what to do. He didn't seem to be like a decisive fellow who would do -- know what to do. A little bit uncertain, insecure. And my impression was that he didn't have much combat experience, and this went for the same unit, the people who were there. And I said quite loudly that nobody should approach the building, and that his soldiers could open fire freely to -- on anyone who attempted to approach the building. And if he needed it, he could call me and that we would then deal with that, with those -- any attackers. So the reason why I did that was to instill some security in him; and if anyone had been there in the dark, that person could then hear that. "So let me explain to you now, there were quite a few locals there. I didn't see them. But there were quite a few of those locals there who had parents, brothers, sisters killed, and they were pretty tense. And all of them knew what unit we were, and I don't think that anyone would have wanted to get into conflict with us. Then I decided to get into the hangar for the simple reason because I wanted to see whether any of my former subordinates or soldiers were there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree -- would you agree that those were your words?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So unlike your testimony of yesterday, he didn't -- the lieutenant-colonel didn't just tell you there was some prisoners in the hangar, he told you when you first spoke to him that there was some problems and that there was some dangers there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said that he thought there were some danger, not -- so if you play it back, you will see that I said that he thought there were some problems, and if -- yesterday, I said that there had been no problems, and the only thing that is evident from what he said was that he thought that there had been some problems. I didn't want to get into that any further. Because yesterday during our conversation, I noticed this tendency, your younger colleague was there, I said that Mrksic had sent me to check there and then he asked me, "So, Mrksic sent you there to protect these people." So there is this tendency to interpret my responses, to exploit this small uncertainty, to establish a position where I would be in an untenable position. So I still maintain what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you know -- sir, he told you -- if you don't want to say he told you directly, he told you that he believed that there were some problems; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that he believed, but he thought -- okay. Okay. Believed, that's fine. That term can go used. But if somebody believes that there are problems, it doesn't mean that there are problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as a result, you issued an order that the soldiers can shoot anyone who approaches the hangars or the hangar, or the building, or whatever word you want to use. Isn't that is correct? That's the order you issued?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not issue an order. I said that I had said aloud to him and to his soldiers that they could fire. I did not issue an order. Again, I have to repeat: You stated that I said to my soldiers, and here you could hear that I said "to his soldiers." This was not an order but an instruction, because I did not have the authority to issue orders to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You issued an instruction. This is again what you didn't testify to yesterday. You issued an instruction to shoot anyone who approached the hangars. You didn't testify to that yesterday either, did you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give you an interpretation of the conversation. I merely told you that I spoke with that person, Mr. Bulatovic warned me to be brief and I didn't go into those details. And this was a conversation of five to ten minutes, so we must have talked about something. And this is what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You also didn't testify that you gave that instruction in a loud voice so that if anyone was out there, they would hear the instruction not to come near the hangar; isn't that true too? You didn't say that yesterday either.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't talk about that yesterday. If I didn't tell you what I had told him, I couldn't have told you that this was done in a loud voice. But I can tell you now and tell the Court, again, that I -- the reason why I said that was to instill some confidence in him, to make him less insecure. That was the main reason more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also indicate in your statement that there were locals who were tense and who were interested in revenge because their family members had been killed. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were some locals; but again, I said that it was not at that specific location, but in the general area. I said that there was a possibility, but that I did not see anyone there, and then I explained as to what kind of people we could be dealing with. There were people who wanted revenge in the Vukovar area, so I -- in fact, I specifically said "not there." Hypothetically speaking, yes, you could assume that some people might show up there, but there were no such people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, unlike your testimony yesterday, there was a five- to ten-minute conversation relating to a threat or danger at Ovcara; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conversation took about ten minutes, and this is what we were talking about in general. He said that there were prisoners there, that he set-up the security, and so on. So in the ten minutes, we did touch upon that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you then went into the hangar; and while in the hangar, you saw 60 to 70 prisoners or 60 to 80.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said 60, 70, 80. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it possible that there were two or three times that number? There were 150, 175 prisoners, say 175 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 175 [as interpreted], no, that's impossible. Perhaps more than the figure that I gave you, but nobody can really give you an exact figure. It's more an assessment, an approximation. I didn't stay there for long enough to count them. They were all hunkered down next to the wall; but 275 people, you would need a larger space for that. Maybe 120, but may assessment was 80, 60, 70, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this is important. Page 72, line 14, at the beginning of the response, the witness mentioned the figure 275; and then said, "no, that's impossible," and the transcript reads 175. Line 13, again should read 275 and the witness received the interpretation 275.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I received interpretation 275, yet the transcript reads 175.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I can clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I put to you that there were 175 prisoners there; one, seven, five, do you agree with that or disagree?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not go down that lane. My memory tells me that there were maybe 60 to 80 people there, as I told you. And I wouldn't now venture whether there might have been 175, because I did not count them. And it was not really possible to do that, to make an accurate estimation as to their number, whether it was 175.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, according to testimony of one of the security members that was there, there were 175 prisoners from the Mitnica group on November 18th.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No comment. I don't know whether this is really so or not so. I can't really comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry about that. So you stayed there for a while and then left, sir. Are you familiar with a police officer or a military police officer, military police commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade by the name of Vesmarevic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Am I familiar with him, or do I know him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: According to testimony, he was in charge of the security there throughout the evening. You never saw him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember him. I only talked to lieutenant-colonel. It was dark, and there were other people there, soldiers, some other people. They had the same uniform, olive drab uniform, officers and soldiers. So in the dark, it's hard to tell who is an officer, who is a soldier unless you know the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that Vesmarevic, the commander of the 80th military police, was there all evening and never mentions you being there or never mentions the anti-terrorist unit arriving that evening? Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would that surprise me? If he wasn't there, then he was unable to see me, because I didn't see him. So I said that he wasn't there, or rather, that I didn't see him. Most likely, he wasn't there so then there's no wonder that he didn't see me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you if Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic of the 80th Motorised Brigade indicates that he never -- has never testified that he met you on the evening of the 18th of November, or that your unit appeared on the evening of the 18th of November? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense you mean. I told you that there was a lieutenant-colonel there who told me that he was the commander. Now whether that was Vojnovic or some other lieutenant-colonel, I don't know. That would surprise me if, indeed, that was Vojnovic, if he said that I wasn't present, that I didn't come. I could only conclude that he either forgot about me coming or that he doesn't want that to be known. I am prepared to face him and to establish whether that is the man that I remember seeing or not and whether I was there or not. In addition, you can also ask the Croats who were there. They will certainly tell you. Naturally, they won't tell you that it was me with my name, but they will tell you that there were large built people in camouflage uniforms with helmets and so on and that that scared them. You will definitely be able to establish that on that night, we were there. Now, as to whether seeing Vezmarevic or Vojnovic is more important than seeing some 20 of us and the Croats, well, it's up to you to judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an officer by the name of Danilovic from the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anyone from the 80th Motorised Brigade, because the only contact with had with them was on that night. Afterwards, I never saw any one of them, and I didn't know any of them. I don't know a single person from the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Officer Radoje Danilovic was also there throughout the evening, and it was a quiet evening, according to his testimony. He was a Defence witness. And he never places you or your unit there, does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I don't know the man. The same answer as the one I gave you for Vezmarevic. I would be surprised if Filip Karaula were to say that I wasn't there, because I'm sure he remembers well that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, the three people overseeing the evacuation at Ovcara, Vojnovic, Vezmarevic and Danilovic, never mention you being there. Is it possible you weren't there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's impossible. I was there just as I am sure that I am sitting here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May we go into private session, Your Honour, for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at ten minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, may the witness please be shown this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has something, Mr. Weiner, if I can interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't even have a proposal, just to consult the Chamber. Mr. Weiner said that he would have another 20 minutes, and Mr. Bulatovic indicated that he would have another half an hour. Now, the witness has been here since 2.00, and now I don't know what we should do, whether we should release this witness and then -- and bring Mr. Stojic in and then start anew tomorrow when we are all fresh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we could even start an hour earlier tomorrow if that would make you happy. No, we will not start the new witness this evening, given that we have only just over an hour remaining. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I'd like to show you this photograph and put it on the ELMO, and that comes from a video, Exhibit 850. And I just want to ask if it's you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not me. And to avoid any doubts, I can give you a few facts that will prove this. This person is wearing an olive drab JNA uniform, and he has a vest over it. I wore a camouflage uniform. This is an ordinary JNA helmet that this person is wearing, and my unit wore helmets, Swiss made PSH helmets that looked completely different. This person has at least one month growth of beard, and I had arrived in Vukovar on the 10th in October and I couldn't have grown the beard that long. I have longer beard now than I had at the time. And now the question that I am interested in is why would anyone think that this was me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, just a question on your answer: "I had arrived in Vukovar on the 10th, and it says in October. You were not in the -- in Vukovar on the 10th of October; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't in October. It was -- it was on the 10th of November. I came back in -- sometime between the 5th and the 10th of November, and I would not have gotten back with the beard. And I couldn't have grown a beard in -- until the 20th. And now I just want to ask you the question: Why would you think this is me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I really don't have to answer the question; however, I would say it looks like you and the voice in the video sounds just like yours. So that's why we wanted to inquire whether or not it was you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware -- or actually, you testified that it was quiet on November 18th at Ovcara. Were you aware that they had troubles in the afternoon of November 20th at Ovcara? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that locals, when the buses arrived with the prisoners, that locals formed a gauntlet. And they beat with their hands and with their fists and with their rifle butts, the prisoners. As they got off the bus, that they beat them? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know that they had gone to Ovcara. I know that they had left the barracks when I left the barracks. But I didn't know where they had gone to; and, least of all, did I know what -- that such a thing might have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that local soldiers, meaning local TOs and volunteers had beaten, at least inside the hangar, one prisoner seriously, one or more prisoners seriously? One was beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that Colonel Vojnovic of the 80th Motorised Brigade tried to protect some of the prisoners as they were getting off the bus and was assaulted? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But would you agree, sir, that that type of situation, an attack on prisoners and even the murder of one, was the type of situation where your unit or military police units would be activated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified on the 19th, you and a few other officers removed 50 - you called them a motley group - from the barracks, without force on the 19th; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 19th, it was on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you did that without any serious difficulty; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you agree that a group of local TO members and volunteers were no match for the Guards Motorised Brigade, military police, or anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were no match for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you would agree that your unit is specially trained for rapid responses, hostage situations, dealing with terrorist or paramilitary organisations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the unit was trained for and that was its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So that evening, if you received an order to protect those prisoners on a 24-hour basis, beginning in the early evening through the morning of the 21st of November, did you have the manpower to do so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- the question is not defined enough in terms of what kind of danger. If you had an attack by 2.000 people, then I could not have done anything. But if it's an attack by maybe 20 to 30 people, then, yes, I could do something. I couldn't have done anything in case of attack by people carrying heavy weapons, and I could do something if these people carried only infantry weapons or knives. So you have to be very specific what kind of danger are you referring to as being present there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's take a group of 25 to 50 TO members or volunteers with infantry weapons, small arms. If you and the military police battalion or battalions were ordered to that area to guard those prisoners and protect them on a 24-hour basis until they were removed from the area, did you have the manpower, weaponry, ammunition to do so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did for such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that you didn't have any other tasks on the 20st or 21st which would have prevented you from accomplishing that task of protecting those prisoners, if ordered to do so.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we received any other tasks, we would have done this if we had been ordered to do so. But I know that we did not have any specific tasks in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, were you aware of any problem with the communication system or the reporting system at the command on November 20th?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nor was there any reason for me to be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, when we were in closed session, we spoke of two matters, which you testified here for the first time today, and I want to put it to you that you made those facts up today to help your friends, who are the accused here. Please respond.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Those facts that we discussed just before the break, which I indicated that you testified for the first time and that had never told anyone previously about those facts. I put to you that you made those up today to help your friends, the accused.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what's your foundation for making this claim; but now that you tell me that (redacted) had testified and that he said that he had been there, I can say that he invented that. He could not have received his orders from anyone apart from me. And he couldn't have gotten it through any other part of the chain of command, because he was in contact only with me. He could not have involved any other people or engaged any other people, because all the cars and all the people were under my control. And I want to know; I want to see the list: Who were those people that went with him that night? Now that you told me, I understand what you're talking about. I understand why this whole thing is focussing on this, because this is a fabricated event because. And I'm ready to confront both him and all the other people. So I want to see them face to face, and then we can perhaps determine what happened. We can bring all the people who were there and hear their testimony apart from him. And now I know why you asked me questions about him, whether he was honest, but -- and I did confirm that he was a good officer, but the other people are -- were better than he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He was an honest man. You confirmed, too. As long as you knew him, he was an honest man. And I put to you, sir, that you--

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. He was. But if he did, in fact, invent this, then he -- I don't think that he is an honest man any more, and people are perishable goods. And I have to say that he invented this. I did not invent anything. I may be confused about some small details, but the relevant events, relevant for you, this is how they played out from the point of view of myself and my unit. I could talk to you and hours and prove to you that (redacted) could not have gone there. And even had he wanted to, he -- the people would not have gone with him, the personnel. I think that this thing that you just said, I take it as a personal insult, the thing that you just said that I invented things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I put to you that he went there on the evening of the 20th, because that was the only day that it was a -- there was a need to activate the anti-terrorist unit. That's what I put to you, sir. There wasn't a need on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he went there, why didn't he intervene? This was not our want to go some place and not to carry out our task. And I asked you whether you had anyone else corroborating this, apart from him. Who gave him this task, and I didn't. I would have known, had I given him this task. And you can always -- you can always see from my past actions that I always went with my unit into the thick of things. I would never have sent them there to go on their own, and I would like to get this information who ordered him to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A Mr. Bajic; and further, sir, he was ordered to leave?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bajic who?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Commander Bajic; and he was ordered to leave.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he received orders from Bajic? Bajic was a nobody there then. So how -- how and what chain of command was Bajic his superior, his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I put it to you he was sent there, and he was ordered to leave by the command. And you -- and, sir, you weren't there, so you can't even say what happened there because you weren't there; isn't that correct? You weren't in Ovcara on that day. You were not in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I was not on the 20th. I was not there on the 20th and he was not there. So he claims that Adem Bajic ordered him to go there, and just the two of them know about this thing and nobody else. And probably they have something in writing to corroborate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you weren't there; and unless you have clairvoyance, you can't tell who else was there. And I put it to you, he was there on that night. And you're wrong or you're lying when you say he wasn't, and you're doing that to protect the people you've known for many years.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may be clairvoyant, but he probably is gifted with bi-location. And he is probably able to multiply people so they can be with him and with me at the same time. And he was probably here executing orders from Bajic, and Bajic had nothing to do with us. Perhaps the postman came by and sent him there. And you tell me that I'm lying, and I tell you that you're manipulating facts. And I believe that you probably blackmailed him with some visa, things to get a visa or not, and then he testified to the way you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you just lying some more, or do you have any proof if you're going to make an acquisition that I've committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, that will do.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were the first to accuse me of committing a crime. Do you have evidence for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, your testimony, sir.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense is that proof? Do you have (redacted) and now his word should be worth more than mine. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's up for the court to determine. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I would now comment on the words commented by my colleague, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Maric, during the discussion with the OTP representatives yesterday, did you answer all the questions asked to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And now I see that I actually went into too many details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did the OTP representatives, in the course of that interview, show you any document, any photograph, or anything else to elicit your comments, your clarification?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did the OTP representatives yesterday, during that interview, show to you any testimony by any witness.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Maric, about -- how your testimony started yesterday? What was the first question?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really. The first question was my personal details, my name, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How did the interview begin? What was the first topic broached in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lost my concentration. I cannot focus anymore. I think that the first question was about the participation of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was the name of any officers from your unit mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just (redacted), or rather, Mr. Weiner asked me about (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, the Prosecutor asked you whether your company was capable of dealing with that kind of a problem that arose at Ovcara. Let me ask you, in principle, did you know what a military police company means?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? It's a unit numbering about 100 men, people of "A" category. That's how they used to categorise them, which means that the mental and physical capabilities were top at the time. And the programme within military police was the strongest programme in the JNA, except for special forces. So that was quite a strong unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that a military police company could have dealt with the same problem, as it was described to you by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is to say about 50 men, likely armed, should have dealt with that without a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If that military police company is composed of people from reserve forces, would that affect the quality of the unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reserve forces of the military police can be even better than active forces. Because in the reserve forces, there were people who were about 30 years of age. And nobody could have joined reserve forces if they hadn't been in active training. So that this means that these people had been through a lot and they matured, unlike the young soldiers who can have various level of training. It's just a question of the commander, whether the commander is up to it. If he is an active commander in the military police forces, then he should be up to the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th when you talked at Ovcara with that officer, who introduced himself as the commanding officer in the unit, did you know what unit it was, whether it was a unit from active forces, reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have specific information. But given how he was dressed and that he -- his appearance was proper, I concluded that he was a member of active forces. He looked the way an officer or a commanding officer within the JNA ought to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did this JNA officer, on that occasion, after telling you that he thought that there might be some problems, did he complain to you that he didn't have sufficient men in order to resolve this problem that he thought might potentially arise?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this term is unfortunate, "complain." I used that term -- it was simply that in the conversation, he told me these things. He didn't tell me that he needed me to stay. Had he told me that, I would have stayed. So I think that I may have unfortunately used this term "complain." It was simply a conversation and we said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, how many men are there in a military police company?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A full establishment strength should be 100 men. It should have 100 men, 117 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I put this question in order to correct the transcript on page 100, line 19, because it says there are 50, so in order to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you said at one point in time that you said loudly that they should fire if somebody approached. "Somebody" meant whom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anybody who was not authorised to be present, so those could have been members of Croatian forces. It wasn't logical to anticipate that a farmer would come by at night, so we could only anticipate that somebody could come with bad intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to put leading questions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well naturally, you know, I didn't have in mind civilians, because I would have -- I would not have said shoot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The question was put to you whether you had a notebook. You said no. Let me ask you this: Did any other of your colleagues, officers keep a notebook?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that Susic, as commander, did have a notebook. I know him from before. He was quite pedantic and he used to keep notebooks, but none of my subordinate officers had any notebooks, none of them did. Let me just explain this. They are individuals and there's no need for them to keep any records, any documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, a photograph was shown to you. The Prosecutor believes that the person in the photograph resembles you and the voice is similar. And you mentioned that this person had an ordinary helmet; whereas, you had PSH helmets. Can you please explain what those are, and what was the equipment of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a helmet made out of armoured steel, and it protects from shrapnel and also infantry weapons. These helmets are of a particular shape. They go all the way up to the forehead, then go down over ears. And they have a microphone on the side, separated. And in the back, there is a jack for wire, so that you can have radio communication while you have it on it. In front, they have a transparent shield; however, we didn't have -- we didn't have that in Vukovar. And normally, one could see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- normally one could see that such a shield was worn by special police forces when dealing with demonstrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you were told that some kind of order was issued by Adem Bajic. That an order was issued to one of your subordinate officers by Adem Bajic. Do you know who Adem Bajic is, and does he have anything to do with the military police company for anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, Adem Bajic was commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion -- or rather, that was the position he held on the 2nd of October. I don't know whether that was true on the 20th of October as well. In Vukovar, the 1st Platoon was never resubordinated to him. On the 2nd of October, I, with my soldiers's platoons, was resubordinated to him, but not the first platoon. So he had no links to us, either horizontal or vertical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, let us go back to this: Who could issue orders to the military police company for anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was me, Captain Susic, and Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I thank you, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions that will be asked of you in this hearing. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here in The Hague, and for the assistance you've been able to give us. You may now, of course, return to your ordinary activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
